column1: binary-search|What conditions make binary search correct, and what is its complexity?|Binary search needs a sorted sequence or an equivalent monotone predicate with a consistent ordering. It halves the search interval for O(log n) comparisons. Sorting an unsorted input first has its own cost, and linked-list traversal can defeat the usual random-access time bound.|sorted~monotone;log;sorting~cost;random~linked|Binary search works on arbitrary unsorted input without preprocessing.|A developer claims binary search makes one lookup in an unsorted million-element array O(log n) overall. Evaluate it.|The search needs ordering first. Sorting costs O(n log n) for standard comparison sorting, so a single one-off lookup may be better served by a linear scan; repeated queries change the tradeoff.|algo-binary|sorted

hash-table|What assumptions underlie average O(1) hash-table lookup?|Expected constant-time lookup depends on hashing, load factor, collision handling, and key costs. Worst-case collision patterns can degrade performance; resizing has amortized cost. Security-sensitive exposed keys may need collision-resistant hashing policy or other mitigations.|average~expected;collision;load~resiz;worst|Every hash-table lookup has guaranteed worst-case constant time.|A service stores attacker-controlled keys and CPU grows sharply despite a hash map. What should be investigated?|Inspect collision behavior, key hashing cost, load/capacity, and implementation protections. Do not infer worst-case constant performance merely from average-case complexity.|algorithms|Hash

lru|How can an LRU cache support O(1) lookup and recency updates?|Use a hash map from key to node and a doubly linked list for recency. Move a hit to the most-recent end and evict the least-recent node when capacity is exceeded. Specify capacity/weight, updates, thread safety, and absent-key behavior.|hash~map;doubly~linked;evict;recen|A queue without key-to-node lookup guarantees O(1) arbitrary recency updates.|Design an LRU where get must refresh recency and put must update existing keys without duplication.|Locate nodes through the map, unlink/relink in O(1), update an existing node rather than adding duplicates, and remove both map and list entries during eviction. Test capacity zero and repeated updates.|algorithms|Linked

heap|When is a binary heap preferable to sorting an entire task queue for every insertion?|A binary heap supports O(log n) insertion and extract-min/max and O(1) access to its extremum. It is not a fully sorted array and arbitrary lookup is not generally O(log n). Use a separate index for update-by-ID when needed.|log;extrem~minimum~maximum;not~arbitrary;index~queue|Every arbitrary item can be found in a heap in logarithmic time.|An expiring-task scheduler repeatedly sorts all deadlines after each new task. Propose a more suitable structure.|Use a min-heap ordered by deadline; inspect the minimum to schedule wake-up and pop expired tasks. Handle cancellation with an index or lazy invalidation and test equal deadlines and clock behavior.|algo-heap|heap

bfs-dfs|When does BFS find a shortest path, and why is DFS different?|BFS explores vertices by unweighted edge distance using a queue and finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph. DFS follows depth using a stack or recursion and does not generally give shortest paths. Both need visited-state handling to avoid repeated traversal in cyclic graphs.|unweighted;queue;DFS~depth;visited~cycle|DFS always finds the shortest path in any graph.|A navigation graph has all edge costs equal and cycles. Choose a search and define a test oracle.|Use BFS with a visited set and predecessor map. Check that returned edges exist, endpoints are correct, and path length matches a small trusted shortest-distance oracle.|algorithms|Graph

dijkstra|What assumptions does Dijkstra's algorithm require?|Dijkstra's usual correctness argument requires nonnegative edge weights. It expands the smallest tentative distance using a priority queue, updates neighbors, and handles stale queue entries or decrease-key. Negative edges require a different algorithm or justified transformation.|nonnegative~non-negative;priority~heap;distance;negative|Dijkstra is guaranteed correct with arbitrary negative-weight edges.|A graph includes a negative edge and a shortest-path implementation uses Dijkstra. What should change?|Do not rely on Dijkstra's normal guarantee. Assess negative cycles and use an appropriate method such as Bellman-Ford for the required graph and constraints.|algorithms|graph

amortized|How is amortized append complexity different from worst-case append complexity for a dynamic array?|Geometric capacity growth makes a sequence of appends amortized O(1), but an append that reallocates and copies elements can cost O(n). Amortized analysis is not a probability guarantee or a per-operation latency bound; memory overhead is part of the tradeoff.|amortized;realloc~copy;O(n)~linear;latency|Amortized constant time means no individual append is linear.|A latency-sensitive service sees rare long append pauses while average throughput is good. Explain and mitigate it.|Capacity expansion may copy a large buffer. Reserve appropriate capacity, bound batch sizes, or choose a structure suited to latency constraints, then measure tail latency and memory usage.|algorithms|array

sql-index|How should a composite B-tree index be chosen for a PostgreSQL query?|Match equality/range predicates and ordering to the index's column order and operator support, then verify with an execution plan on representative data. Indexes speed some reads but cost storage and write work; selectivity and workload determine whether the planner uses them.|column~order;predicate~equality~range;plan~EXPLAIN;write~storage|Adding every possible index always improves every workload.|A tenant-scoped feed filters tenant_id and orders by created_at and id. Propose an index and verification plan.|Consider a composite index on tenant_id, created_at, id in suitable order for the query, add stable tie handling, and inspect EXPLAIN/ANALYZE with representative cardinalities and write costs.|postgres-index-types|B-tree

sql-null|How does SQL NULL affect equality and NOT IN predicates?|NULL represents unknown, so ordinary equality with NULL is not true; use IS NULL where appropriate. NOT IN can evaluate to unknown when the candidate set includes NULL, unexpectedly filtering rows. Use a correctly correlated NOT EXISTS or explicit NULL policy when that is the intended meaning.|unknown;IS NULL;NOT IN;NOT EXISTS|NULL equals NULL in ordinary SQL equality.|A query using NOT IN returns no rows after a subquery starts returning NULL. Explain a safe rewrite.|Unknown comparisons propagate through NOT IN. Use NOT EXISTS with the intended key correlation or exclude NULL under a justified policy, and test empty, NULL, and matching subquery cases.|postgres-null|NULL

sql-join|Why can a WHERE filter on the nullable side change a LEFT JOIN's result?|A LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched left rows by producing NULL right-side columns. A WHERE predicate that requires a right-side value can remove those rows, producing inner-join-like behavior. Put the matching restriction in ON when unmatched left rows should remain.|NULL;WHERE;ON;unmatched|WHERE and ON are always interchangeable for outer joins.|Return every customer and only their paid invoices, including customers with no paid invoice. Where should the status predicate go?|Use LEFT JOIN invoices ON customer key AND invoice status is paid, then avoid a WHERE predicate that rejects the NULL-extended invoice row. Test no-invoice and only-unpaid cases.|postgres-joins|outer

sql-window|How do window functions differ from grouped aggregation?|A grouped aggregate collapses rows into groups, while a window function computes across a partition/window without necessarily collapsing input rows. ORDER BY and the frame definition affect running totals and peer behavior; use an outer query when filtering a derived window result.|partition;row~collaps;frame;ORDER|Window functions always collapse each partition to a single row.|For each tenant, return the latest event while retaining the original event columns. Give a deterministic strategy.|Assign row_number over partition by tenant ordered by timestamp descending and a stable unique tie-breaker, then filter rn=1 in an outer query. Define behavior for ties and null timestamps.|postgres-window|partition

pagination|What makes keyset pagination different from offset pagination?|Keyset pagination continues after a stable ordered key tuple, commonly with a unique tie-breaker. Large offsets require skipping earlier rows and can shift under concurrent writes. Keyset access can be efficient with a matching index but makes arbitrary page jumps harder and still needs a consistency policy.|key~cursor;tie~unique;offset;index~consisten|A timestamp-only cursor is always unique and stable.|A feed has duplicate timestamps and inserts occur while paging. Design a cursor and continuation predicate.|Order by timestamp plus unique ID, encode/bind the last key tuple and tenant/filter scope, and use a matching lexicographic continuation. Document how new inserts and deletions affect the view.|postgres-limit,postgres-index-types|ORDER BY

atomic-sql|How can a database decrement inventory without a check-then-update race?|Use an atomic conditional update such as UPDATE inventory SET available=available-1 WHERE id=$1 AND available>0 RETURNING available, and check affected rows. Combine related business state with a transaction and constraints; retries of the entire operation still require idempotency.|atomic;WHERE;RETURNING~affected;transaction~idempot|Reading available then issuing an unconditional decrement prevents overselling.|Write the behavior for buying one item when inventory may concurrently reach zero.|Execute a conditional decrement in the same transaction as the order state and treat no affected row as unavailable. Add request idempotency so replay does not buy twice.|postgres,aws-idempotency|UPDATE

promise-all|What happens to other operations when Promise.all rejects?|Promise.all rejects when one input promise rejects, but already-started operations are not automatically cancelled. Preserve results with allSettled when appropriate, and use cooperative cancellation plus explicit resource cleanup when stopping work is required.|reject;not~doesn't~cannot;cancel;allSettled~cleanup|Promise.all automatically cancels every remaining request after one rejection.|Three writes start in Promise.all and the first rejects. Can the caller assume the other writes did not commit?|No. They may still run or commit. Define partial-success handling, idempotency, compensation or a database transaction appropriate to the operations; cancellation cannot undo a completed side effect.|js-promises,aws-idempotency|reject

complexity-output|Why must complexity analysis include input representation and output size?|The cost model includes reading the representation, allocating or emitting results, and relevant operations such as hashing or comparison. An algorithm producing k items requires at least output-proportional work. State average/worst/amortized assumptions and space ownership rather than only naming Big-O.|output;representation~input;assum~worst;space|An algorithm emitting every one of n results can have O(1) total time.|A function scans all rows, builds an output array, and claims O(1) space because it uses one loop variable. Evaluate it.|Auxiliary loop state may be constant, but the returned array occupies output-proportional space. State whether output space is excluded and include the full scan in runtime complexity.|algorithms|complexity
